# 12:00 ALERT decline rate 85%, 940 attempts/h, tiny amounts
# 13:00 ALERT decline rate 88%, 1210 attempts/h, tiny amounts
# 14:00 ok
blocks.caption: Synthetic hourly checkout stats. An alert needs two of: a decline rate far above baseline, a volume spike, tiny amounts.

blocks.title: Decline rate by hour: card testing in a synthetic day

scenes.caption: A normal morning: about 5 to 6% of payment attempts are declined (insufficient funds, typos, expired cards).
12:00 to 14:00: a script runs stolen cards at USD 1. Decline rate jumps to 85% and 88%, attempts rise to 940 and 1,210 an hour.
After a server-verified challenge on the payment endpoint and a per-IP limit on new customers, 14:00 is back to 5.6%.

blocks.md:
**Stopping it.** Stripe's guidance, in short: use an integration with built-in protection; require a CAPTCHA, verified on the server, on *every* request that can validate a card or pay; make the payment form harder to reach (require login or a valid session; CSRF tokens also help); add rate limits shaped to the attack, for example a cap on new customers created from one IP address per day; combine them, so a first payment from an address is easy but repeats need a challenge; and do not keep retrying cards saved by fraudulent customers afterwards, which repeats the attack. Refund suspicious small payments that got through, to avoid disputes.

Card testers can also call the provider directly with your **publishable key**, which is public by design, so limits must live in your server and the provider's controls, not in the key's secrecy.

**3-D Secure.** **EMV 3DS** (EMV 3-D Secure, the version of the 3-D Secure protocol specified by EMVCo) lets the issuer authenticate the cardholder during an online payment. [EMVCo](https://www.emvco.com/emv-technologies/3-d-secure/) describes it as a data exchange between merchant and issuer about the transaction, payment method and device. Most payments are **frictionless**: the issuer judges the data low risk and approves silently. Risky ones get a **challenge**, such as approval in the bank's app.

In the EU and UK, **SCA** (strong customer authentication), required by **PSD2** (the second Payment Services Directive), makes this mandatory for most customer-initiated online payments: two of knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have) and inherence (something you are). The issuer decides whether to grant exemptions for low-risk payments. Per [Stripe](https://stripe.com/guides/strong-customer-authentication), a successfully authenticated payment can shift fraud-dispute liability away from the business; an exemption keeps it with the business.

blocks.title: 3-D Secure at checkout: frictionless or challenged

scenes.caption: Before authorising, the merchant sends 3DS data (amount, device, shipping address, account age) through the network to the issuer's authentication service.
Frictionless: the issuer recognises the device and pattern and authenticates without asking the cardholder anything.
Challenge: for a risky payment the issuer asks the cardholder to confirm in their banking app. A thief with only the card number fails here.
Only then does normal authorisation run. A fraud dispute on an authenticated payment is generally the issuer's loss, not the merchant's.

blocks.md: Card testing costs you even when every attempt is declined. Protect every endpoint that can touch a card with server-verified challenges and shaped rate limits, and use 3-D Secure to move risky card-not-present payments onto the issuer's authentication.

blocks.question: During card testing almost every attempt is declined. Why does the merchant still suffer?
options: A high decline rate makes issuers and networks treat the business as riskier, raising declines for real customers; fees and disputes from the few that succeed add up
The card network bans the merchant on the first attack
blocks.explain: Stripe lists reputation with issuers, fees, disputes on successful tests, load and polluted metrics. The decline-rate damage can outlast the attack.

blocks.question: Your checkout already shows a CAPTCHA, verified on the server. Card testing continues through the 'save card for later' endpoint. What is the most likely gap?
options: The challenge is not required on every request that can validate a card, so attackers use the unprotected one
Card testers solve CAPTCHAs by hand
blocks.explain: Stripe's first check is that the challenge covers all requests that enable card validation or payment. Card setup is a favourite because validations there often do not show on statements.

lessons.title: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order

blocks.md:
A **dispute** is a cardholder contesting a payment with their issuer. When the issuer takes the money back from the merchant through the card network, that is a **chargeback** (the charge is sent back). Reasons include fraud ("I did not make this purchase") and commercial problems (not received, not as described). For fraud teams, the fraud chargeback is the main **label**: the moment you learn, for certain, that a payment was bad.

**Friendly fraud** is the awkward case: the real cardholder disputes a purchase they did make, or that a family member made. It looks like fraud in the data and is labelled as fraud, but no stolen card was involved, so models and rules trained on it learn the wrong lesson unless you separate it.

Stripe's [description of the lifecycle](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/how-disputes-work):

- **Early fraud warnings** (EFWs) come from issuers' fraud reports on the Visa, Mastercard and JCB networks (Visa TC40 and Mastercard SAFE reports). About 40% of Visa and Mastercard EFWs become fraud disputes if you do not refund.
- **Inquiries** (used mostly by American Express and Discover) ask for clarification first; ignoring one can escalate to a chargeback you likely cannot win.
- A **chargeback** debits the amount plus a dispute fee straight away. Cardholders can typically dispute within **120 days** of the payment, longer in some cases, and for future events and services the window starts on the event date.
- The merchant can submit **evidence**; the issuer then usually decides within 60 to 75 days. The full cycle often takes 2 to 3 months.

blocks.title: One fraudulent order, from payment to a lost dispute (synthetic dates)

scenes.caption: Day 0: the order is approved and shipped. To every system it looks like a good sale.
Day 12: the real cardholder reports the charge to their bank; the issuer files a fraud report, which reaches the merchant as an early fraud warning.
Day 35: the chargeback arrives; amount and fee are debited. Day 42: the merchant submits evidence.
About day 110: the issuer rules for the cardholder. Only now is the label final, months after the model scored the order. Most of the delay is invisible to a model in training.

blocks.md: **What a fraudulent order really costs.** The payment is pulled back, so you never keep the revenue. But the goods are gone, the shipping is spent, and the dispute fee is charged. Using synthetic numbers for a USD 80 order:

blocks.code:
# Synthetic order economics (all USD; fee is illustrative, it varies)
price, goods_cost, shipping, dispute_fee = 80.0, 50.0, 8.0, 15.0

margin_good_order = price - goods_cost - shipping
# A fraudulent order: the payment is pulled back by the chargeback,
# the goods are gone, shipping was paid, and the dispute fee is charged.
loss_fraud_order = goods_cost + shipping + dispute_fee

print("margin on a good order :", margin_good_order)
print("loss on a fraud order  :", loss_fraud_order)
print("good orders to recover one fraud:",
      round(loss_fraud_order / margin_good_order, 1))

# Refunding a flagged order yourself avoids the fee and a dispute on your
# record, but the goods and shipping are already gone:
print("loss if refunded before a dispute:", goods_cost + shipping)
# output:
# margin on a good order : 22.0
# loss on a fraud order  : 73.0
# good orders to recover one fraud: 3.3
# loss if refunded before a dispute: 58.0
blocks.caption: Synthetic order economics. One fraudulent order wipes out the margin on more than three good ones.

blocks.md:
That ratio drives everything downstream: losing USD 73 to fraud costs as much as turning away about 3.3 honest USD 80 orders. Lesson 16 uses exactly these two numbers to set thresholds.

**Dispute rates are monitored.** The card networks run [monitoring programmes](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/monitoring-programs) with fees and, at worst, loss of card acceptance. Visa's VAMP (Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program) counts early fraud warnings even if refunded, and separately counts card testing ("enumeration") attempts, approved or declined. That is why card testing and friendly fraud matter even when each amount is small.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: clear billing descriptors (so customers recognise the charge), easy refunds and responsive support (many "fraud" disputes are confused customers), 3-D Secure where risky. *Detect*: track EFWs and dispute rates daily, by product and channel. *Respond*: refund EFWs where Stripe's analysis says it pays (it suggests mainly on charges at or below your dispute fee), fight disputes you can document, and feed every outcome back as a label.

Do not train on chargebacks as if they arrived on the day of the payment. Recent payments look clean simply because their disputes have not arrived yet; a model trained on last week's data learns that last week had no fraud.
Chargebacks are the fraud label, and they arrive weeks to months late. A fraudulent order costs goods, shipping and fees, several good orders' worth of margin.

blocks.question: A model is retrained every Monday on all orders up to the previous Sunday, using 'has a fraud chargeback' as the label. What bias does this create?
options: Recent orders are labelled good because their disputes have not arrived, so the model underestimates fraud in fresh patterns
The model will overestimate fraud on old orders
blocks.explain: Disputes typically arrive over up to 120 days or more. Train on orders old enough for labels to mature, or model label delay explicitly.

blocks.question: With goods cost USD 50, shipping USD 8, price USD 80 and dispute fee USD 15, how much does one fraudulent order lose, and how many good orders' margin does that equal?
blocks.explain: Goods 50 + shipping 8 + fee 15 = 73. A good order earns 80 - 50 - 8 = 22. 73 / 22 is about 3.3. USD 58 is the loss if you refund before a dispute, avoiding the fee.

lessons.title: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review

blocks.md:
All the signals so far feed one question per event: **what do we do now?** Most systems compute a **risk score** and map it to actions. Stripe's Radar, for example, gives each payment a score from 0 to 99; [by default](https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation) 65 or above is "elevated" risk (allowed, but can be sent to manual review) and 75 or above is "high" risk (blocked).

The usual menu of actions, from least to most friction:

1. **Allow**.
2. **Step up**: ask for more proof. At login, MFA; at checkout, 3-D Secure; at signup, phone verification.
3. **Review**: hold the action for a human analyst.
4. **Block**.

**Rules or models?** A **rule** is a hand-written condition ("block if more than 5 cards on this device in an hour"). Rules are fast to write, easy to explain and good for a known attack this week. A **model** (logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, neural networks) learns weights over hundreds of signals from labelled history; Stripe says Radar's model uses hundreds of risk factors and learns from feedback when payments are marked fraudulent. Models catch subtler patterns but need labels, monitoring and explanation tools. Real systems use both: a model score, plus rules that use the score, plus rules for new attacks the model has not seen.

**Where to put thresholds.** Turn the score into a probability $p$ that the event is fraud (a **calibrated** score means that among events scored 0.2, about 20% are fraud). Then compare the expected cost of each action, using the numbers from lesson 15.

blocks.caption: L: loss on a fraudulent order (73). G: margin on a good order (22). A step-up catches a share c of fraud (0.9) and loses a share d of good customers who abandon it (0.1).

blocks.code:
# p = model's probability that the order is fraud (synthetic, calibrated)
LOSS_IF_FRAUD = 73.0      # from the chargeback lesson
MARGIN_IF_GOOD = 22.0
STEP_UP_DROP = 0.10       # 10% of good customers abandon a challenge
STEP_UP_CATCH = 0.90      # a challenge stops 90% of fraud

def expected_costs(p):
    allow = p * LOSS_IF_FRAUD
    block = (1 - p) * MARGIN_IF_GOOD                     # good sales lost
    step_up = (p * (1 - STEP_UP_CATCH) * LOSS_IF_FRAUD
               + (1 - p) * STEP_UP_DROP * MARGIN_IF_GOOD)
    return {"allow": allow, "step_up": step_up, "block": block}

for p in (0.01, 0.05, 0.20, 0.50, 0.80):
    c = expected_costs(p)
    best = min(c, key=c.get)
    print(f"p={p:.2f}", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in c.items()}, "->", best)
# output:
# p=0.01 {'allow': 0.73, 'step_up': 2.25, 'block': 21.78} -> allow
# p=0.05 {'allow': 3.65, 'step_up': 2.45, 'block': 20.9} -> step_up
# p=0.20 {'allow': 14.6, 'step_up': 3.22, 'block': 17.6} -> step_up
# p=0.50 {'allow': 36.5, 'step_up': 4.75, 'block': 11.0} -> step_up
# p=0.80 {'allow': 58.4, 'step_up': 6.28, 'block': 4.4} -> block
blocks.caption: Expected cost per order for each action, synthetic numbers. The cheapest action changes with p.

blocks.title: Expected cost per order of allow, step up and block

params.name: d
params.label: good users lost to step-up d

scenes.caption: With only allow and block, the lines cross at p = G/(L+G) = 22/95, about 0.23: block above it, allow below.
Add step-up. It is cheapest from p about 0.032 to about 0.73. A good challenge replaces most blocks and many allows.
If the challenge drives away 30% of good customers (d = 0.3), step-up only wins from about 0.09 to about 0.68: friction has a price.
For a cheap digital item where fraud loses little (L = 25), the allow region grows: thresholds are per product, not universal.

blocks.md:
**Manual review** is expensive and slow, so it belongs where a human adds information: the middle band, large amounts, or new patterns. Give reviewers the reasons behind a score (which signals fired) and record their decisions as labels.

**Explainability.** Every decision should carry **reason codes**: the rule that fired or the top contributing signals. You need them for reviewers, for support conversations, for appeals (lesson 19) and for debugging. "The model said 81" is not a reason anyone can act on.

A score is only a probability if it is calibrated. Raw scores from many models are not; a "0.8" may mean 30% fraud. Calibrate on recent labelled data before you plug scores into expected-cost thresholds.
Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

blocks.question: With L = 73 and G = 22 and no step-up option, above what probability of fraud should you block?
blocks.explain: Block when $(1-p)G < pL$, which gives $p > G/(L+G) = 22/95$, about 0.23. Because fraud costs more than a good sale earns, you block well below 50%.

blocks.question: A new 3-D Secure flow loses 40% of good customers who face it. What happens to the range of scores where step-up is the best action?
options: It narrows, because each challenge now costs more in lost good orders
blocks.explain: The step-up cost term $(1-p)dG$ grows with d, so step-up beats allow only at higher p and beats block only at lower p. Measuring abandonment is part of measuring a control.

lessons.title: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels

blocks.md:
A fraud control makes two kinds of mistake. It lets fraud through (a **false negative**), and it stops an honest user (a **false positive**). Count them in a **confusion matrix** on events whose true label you know:

- **TP** (true positive): fraud, and the control fired.
- **FP** (false positive): good, but the control fired. The rate at which good users are hit is sometimes called the **insult rate**, because that is how it feels to the customer.
- **FN** (false negative): fraud that got through.
- **TN** (true negative): good, and left alone.

blocks.caption: Precision: of what you stopped, how much was fraud. Recall: of all fraud, how much you stopped. FPR (false positive rate): of all good users, how many you hit.

blocks.md:
**Base rates make this hard.** Fraud is rare: the Federal Reserve put US card fraud at under one-tenth of a percent of card payment value (lesson 13). When the bad class is that small, even a tiny false positive rate on the huge good class produces more false positives than there is fraud to catch.

The code simulates 100,000 synthetic orders with 0.5% fraud and a decent model, then measures three thresholds.

blocks.caption: Synthetic scores; seed fixed so the numbers repeat. Low thresholds catch most fraud but mostly hit good users.

blocks.title: Confusion matrix of 100,000 orders at three thresholds

scenes.caption: Threshold 0.5. Top row is the 518 fraud orders: 463 caught, 55 missed (recall 0.89). Bottom row is the good orders: 2,152 blocked. Precision is 463 / 2,615 = 0.18.
Threshold 0.7. Recall falls to 0.58 (299 caught), but blocked good orders fall to 118. Precision is 0.72.
Threshold 0.85. Almost no false positives (1), precision 0.99, but recall 0.22: 403 frauds go through.

blocks.md:
Which threshold is best? Not the highest precision or the highest recall: the lowest total cost. With L = 73 per missed fraud and G = 22 per blocked good order (lesson 15), cost is $73\,FN + 22\,FP$:

- 0.5: 73 x 55 + 22 x 2,152 = **USD 51,359**
- 0.7: 73 x 219 + 22 x 118 = **USD 18,583**
- 0.85: 73 x 403 + 22 x 1 = **USD 29,441**

The middle threshold wins by a wide margin. Track these alongside the classic metrics: **fraud loss rate** (loss as a share of sales), **dispute rate**, **approval rate** for good customers, challenge pass and abandonment rates, and review queue size and time.

**The missing labels.** Two problems make even these numbers hard to get.

**Delay.** The fraud label is usually a chargeback, which arrives weeks or months late (lesson 15). Metrics for last week are not final; report them as "matured" only after the dispute window.

**Selection bias.** You never learn the truth about events you blocked: a blocked order is never shipped, so it can never be charged back. Your measured false positives are therefore guesses, and a model retrained only on allowed events never sees the area it blocks. The standard fix is a small **holdout**: let a tiny random share of events bypass a control and observe what happens. Stripe [says it does this](https://docs.stripe.com/radar/risk-evaluation): for a small subset of payments it modifies the reported risk score so it can measure model performance and keep false positive rate and recall within desirable ranges. The holdout costs a little fraud; it buys the only unbiased estimate you have.

blocks.prompt: Your new rule blocks 1,000 orders a week. Ops says 'none were charged back, so the rule has perfect precision'. What is wrong with that argument?
blocks.reveal: Blocked orders are never shipped or captured, so they cannot be charged back: the absence of chargebacks is guaranteed whether they were fraud or not. To estimate precision you need evidence about blocked events themselves: a random holdout that lets a small share through, analyst review of a sample, or customer complaints and retries. Otherwise you are measuring nothing.

blocks.md: "Fraud went down" can mean the control worked, the attackers moved elsewhere, or labels have not arrived yet. Always read loss together with friction (approval rate, insult rate) and with label maturity.
Choose thresholds by total cost, not by precision or recall alone. Wait for labels to mature, and keep a small random holdout, because blocked events never tell you whether they were fraud.

blocks.question: At a threshold your control has precision 0.18 and recall 0.89 on a base rate of 0.5%. What does precision 0.18 mean for customers?
options: Of the orders you blocked, 82% were from good customers
The model is wrong 18% of the time
blocks.explain: Precision is TP / (TP + FP). At 0.18, only 18% of blocked orders were fraud; the other 82% were honest customers. With rare fraud, even a small false positive rate creates this.

blocks.question: Why does a fraud team keep a small random holdout that bypasses the model?
options: Blocked events never get labels, so a random unblocked sample is needed to measure false positives and recall without bias
blocks.explain: Selection bias: you only observe outcomes for allowed events. A random holdout gives an unbiased view of what the control would have stopped, at a small, known cost. Stripe describes doing this for a small subset of payments.

lessons.title: Fake reviews and content abuse

blocks.md:
Platforms that show user content (reviews, posts, listings, messages) face abuse of what people *see*. Two big families:

- **Inauthentic content**: fake reviews and ratings, bought followers and likes, coordinated campaigns. The harm is deception: people choose products or believe claims because of fake signals.
- **Harmful content**: spam (OWASP OAT-017 Spamming), scams, harassment, and illegal material. The harm is to the people who see it or are depicted in it.

Both meet the same engineering pattern: detect at upload or after, decide, enforce, allow appeal (lesson 19), and learn from the outcomes.

**Fake reviews are now explicitly illegal in the US.** The FTC's **Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials** ([16 CFR Part 465, Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/08/22/2024-18519/trade-regulation-rule-on-the-use-of-consumer-reviews-and-testimonials)), effective 21 October 2024, prohibits among other things: creating, selling or buying fake consumer reviews or testimonials; buying reviews conditioned on their sentiment; undisclosed reviews by company insiders; company-controlled "independent" review sites; certain review suppression; and selling or buying fake indicators of social media influence such as bought followers. The FTC noted reports that generative AI makes fake reviews easier to write.

For platforms this means fake-review detection protects users *and* gives evidence for enforcement against sellers and brokers.

**Detection signals for fake reviews:**

- **Text similarity**: templates and lightly edited copies. Compare reviews with **shingles** (overlapping word sequences) and **Jaccard similarity** (shared items divided by all distinct items).
- **Bursts**: many five-star reviews for one product in hours, often right after launch or after a bad review.
- **Lockstep groups**: the same set of reviewers reviewing the same set of products, a dense block in the reviewer by product matrix, like the rings of lesson 10.
- **Reviewer history**: new accounts, no purchases, reviews only for one seller's products.
- **Verified purchase**: a review tied to a real, completed order costs the faker a purchase.

blocks.code:
def shingles(text, k=3):
    w = text.lower().split()
    return {" ".join(w[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(w) - k + 1)}

def jaccard(a, b):
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b)

reviews = {  # synthetic
    "r1": "great blender works perfectly and the shipping was super fast",
    "r2": "great blender works perfectly and shipping was super fast too",
    "r3": "the lid cracked after two weeks but support replaced it quickly",
}
s = {k: shingles(v) for k, v in reviews.items()}
print("r1~r2", round(jaccard(s["r1"], s["r2"]), 2))
print("r1~r3", round(jaccard(s["r1"], s["r3"]), 2))

# Perceptual hashes (like PDQ's 256 bits; 16 bits here) of three images.
# Similar images give hashes that differ in few bits.
known_bad = 0b1011001110001111
upload_a  = 0b1011001110001101       # a re-encoded copy
upload_b  = 0b0100110001110010       # an unrelated image
for name, h in (("a", upload_a), ("b", upload_b)):
    d = bin(known_bad ^ h).count("1")  # Hamming distance
    print(name, "distance", d, "MATCH" if d <= 2 else "")
# output:
# r1~r2 0.45
# r1~r3 0.0
# a distance 1 MATCH
# b distance 15
blocks.caption: Near-duplicate text by 3-word shingles and Jaccard similarity, and near-duplicate images by Hamming distance between perceptual hashes. All data synthetic; the 16-bit hashes are shortened for display.

blocks.title: Reviewers by products: a lockstep block stands out

scenes.caption: Each 1 is a five-star review. Real reviewers (r1, r2, r6) review scattered products at different times.
Reviewers r3, r4 and r5 all reviewed the same four products (p3 to p6). A dense block like this is the signature of a review ring.
Inside the block: twelve reviews from three accounts over four products. Add timing (same day) and new accounts, and the case for review is strong.

blocks.md:
**Known harmful media: hash matching.** For material already identified as illegal, platforms compare uploads against shared hash lists. A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) changes completely if one pixel changes, so these systems use **perceptual hashes**, which give similar hashes for images that look similar, compared by **Hamming distance** (the number of differing bits).

- **PhotoDNA**, developed by Microsoft with Dartmouth College in 2009, hashes images to find copies of known child sexual exploitation images; [Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/photodna) notes the hash cannot recreate the image. Providers report matches to NCMEC (the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children).
- **PDQ**, open-sourced by Meta in its [ThreatExchange repository](https://github.com/facebook/ThreatExchange/tree/main/pdq), is a 256-bit perceptual hash ([write-up](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/ThreatExchange/main/hashing/hashing.pdf)) based on a discrete cosine transform; its docs suggest starting with a match threshold of Hamming distance 31 or less.

Never build your own collection of illegal material to test a detector. Work with the hash lists, tools and legal reporting channels that exist for this purpose, and route matches to trained staff under your legal team's procedures.

Inauthentic content shows as copies and groups: near-duplicate text, bursts, and lockstep reviewer sets. Known harmful media is matched with perceptual hashes against shared lists, never by collecting it yourself.

blocks.question: Two images differ in 1 bit of their perceptual hashes; their SHA-256 hashes differ in about half their bits. What does this tell you?
options: The images look almost the same (for example a re-encoded copy); a cryptographic hash is designed to change completely on any change
blocks.explain: Perceptual hashes keep similar inputs close in Hamming distance; cryptographic hashes are designed so any change scrambles the output. That is why matching known media uses perceptual hashes.

blocks.question: Which of these does the FTC's 2024 consumer review rule prohibit?
options: Asking all customers for honest reviews
Buying positive reviews or paying for reviews conditioned on their sentiment
blocks.explain: The rule bans creating, buying or selling fake reviews and buying reviews conditioned on their sentiment, among other practices. Asking every customer for an honest review, or responding to reviews, is not prohibited.

lessons.title: Enforcement, explanations and appeals

blocks.md:
Detection decides that something is wrong. **Enforcement** decides what happens to the account, and it is where fraud and abuse systems touch people's livelihoods: a seller's shop, a creator's audience, a user's access to their own photos. Good enforcement is **proportionate** (matched to severity and history), **explained** (the user can see what rule and what facts), **reversible** (mistakes can be undone) and **consistent** (similar cases get similar outcomes).

A common structure is an **enforcement ladder**: warn, then limit features for a time, then suspend, then ban, with severe violations (for example selling stolen cards, or child exploitation) going straight to the top.

blocks.code:
LADDER = ["warn", "limit features 7d", "suspend 30d", "ban"]

def enforce(account, violation, detected_by, history):
    step = min(len(history), len(LADDER) - 1)
    if violation["severity"] == "severe":
        step = len(LADDER) - 1                  # skip straight to the top
    return {                                     # the statement of reasons
        "account": account,
        "action": LADDER[step],
        "rule": violation["rule"],               # which policy, quoted
        "facts": violation["facts"],             # what was seen, not how
        "detected_by": detected_by,
        "decided_by": "person" if step >= 2 else "automated",
        "appeal": "in-app, reviewed by a different person",
    }

v = {"rule": "Spam 2.1: bulk unsolicited messages", "severity": "normal",
     "facts": "412 identical messages to non-contacts on 3 Nov"}
r = enforce("u42", v, "automated", history=[])
print(r["action"], "|", r["decided_by"], "|", r["facts"])
r = enforce("u42", v, "automated", history=["warn", "limit"])
print(r["action"], "|", r["decided_by"])
# output:
# warn | automated | 412 identical messages to non-contacts on 3 Nov
# suspend 30d | person
blocks.caption: A ladder with a record of reasons. Automated decisions are allowed at the low rungs; suspensions and bans get a person before they take effect.

blocks.md: **The law increasingly requires this.** In the EU, the **Digital Services Act** (DSA) requires hosting services to tell users about content moderation decisions and the reasons behind them, in a **statement of reasons**; online platforms submit these statements to the public [DSA Transparency Database](https://transparency.dsa.ec.europa.eu/), which tracks moderation decisions in almost real time. Users can [appeal](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act) a moderation decision through the platform itself or through an out-of-court dispute settlement body. Platforms with over 45 million monthly users in the EU have extra duties to assess and reduce systemic risks.

Data protection law adds a second layer. Under the EU GDPR **Article 22**, people have extra protection from decisions based **solely on automated processing** that have legal or similarly significant effects on them. The UK replaced its copy of Article 22 with Articles 22A to 22D in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, in force from February 2026: such decisions are allowed in more cases, but [only with safeguards](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/data-use-and-access-act-2025-data-protection-and-privacy-changes): telling people about significant decisions, letting them make representations and challenge them, and letting them obtain human intervention.

blocks.title: From detection to a fair outcome, and back to the model

scenes.caption: A rule or model flags an account, and the ladder picks an action based on severity and history.
The user gets a statement of reasons: which policy, what was observed, whether automation was involved, and how to appeal.
On appeal, a person who did not make the first decision reviews it with the evidence.
Either outcome is a label. A rule whose decisions are often reversed on appeal is a precise measure of false positives in the wild.

blocks.md:
**How much to say.** There is a real tension. Users need to know what they did wrong to fix it or contest it, and the law requires reasons. But telling a fraudster "blocked because more than 5 cards on this device in an hour" teaches them to use 4. The usual balance: state the **policy** and the **observed behaviour** ("bulk messages to people who are not your contacts on 3 November"), not the **detector's internals** (thresholds, features, weights).

**Appeals are a measurement tool.** The **overturn rate** per rule or model (share of appealed decisions reversed) is one of the few ground-truth signals you get on false positives, and it covers exactly the cases people cared enough to contest. A rule with a high overturn rate is costing honest users; fix it rather than the appeals queue.
Enforce on a proportionate ladder, give a statement of the policy and behaviour (not the detector's thresholds), let a different person review appeals, and treat overturns as labels.

blocks.question: A user's seller account is banned automatically by a model, with no explanation and no way to reach a person. Which problem is this under EU and UK rules?
options: Lack of a statement of reasons and an appeal route (DSA), and a solely automated decision with significant effects without a way to get human intervention (GDPR Article 22; UK Articles 22A to 22D)
Only a problem if the user is in the US
blocks.explain: The DSA requires reasons and complaint routes for moderation decisions on platforms; Article 22 protections apply to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, which losing a seller account can be.

blocks.question: Which statement of reasons best balances the user's right to understand with not teaching attackers?
options: 'Blocked: risk score 0.91 > threshold 0.85 from features device_cards_1h=6, ip_type=hosting.'
'Suspended for 30 days under Payments policy 3.2 (use of payment cards that are not yours): 6 different cards were added to your account on 3 Nov and declined. You can appeal here.'
No message; silent bans prevent evasion
blocks.explain: It names the policy and the observed behaviour and gives an appeal route, without exposing the score threshold or feature names an attacker could tune against. The first says nothing useful; the second leaks the detector.

lessons.title: Privacy and fairness of risk models

blocks.md:
Fraud systems collect a lot about people: devices, locations, behaviour, links between accounts. That creates two duties that are easy to forget under attack pressure.

**Privacy.** Device fingerprinting is tracking. In the EU, the ePrivacy Directive's Article 5(3) governs storing or accessing information on a user's device; the European Data Protection Board (EDPB, the body of EU data protection authorities) [Guidelines 2/2023](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-22023-technical-scope-art-53-eprivacy-directive_en) on its technical scope recall that the Article 29 Working Party (the EDPB's predecessor) already clarified, in Opinion 9/2014, that fingerprinting falls within that article. Whether consent is needed or an exemption applies (for example, a service the user explicitly requested) is a legal question for your counsel; the engineering duties are clear either way.

**Engineering for privacy in fraud systems:**

- **Minimise**: collect the signals that measurably improve decisions, not everything a browser exposes. Lesson 6's entropy view helps: a few high-entropy attributes often do the job.
- **Separate purpose**: data collected for fraud prevention should not quietly flow into advertising.
- **Limit retention**: keep raw signals for the label window plus investigation time, then aggregate or delete.
- **Pseudonymise carefully**: hashing a phone number or email does not anonymise it (the space is small and can be enumerated, lesson 4); the course *Privacy engineering* covers why.
- **Restrict access**: risk data reveals movements and relationships; log who looks at it.

**Fairness.** A risk model can hurt some groups of honest users far more than others, even with no protected attribute (such as ethnicity or nationality) among its inputs, because other signals act as **proxies** (stand-ins) for it. Network signals are a classic example: users on **CGNAT** mobile networks or in shared places (campuses, libraries) share IP addresses with many strangers, so "many accounts per IP" fires on them. If such users are concentrated in particular countries or income groups, the burden lands there.

Moritz Hardt, Eric Price and Nathan Srebro formalised one fairness criterion in "[Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02413)" (2016): equal true positive rates across groups (their stricter criterion, **equalized odds**, also asks for equal false positive rates). For fraud friction, the mirror image is usually the one to watch: **equal false positive rates**, meaning honest users in every group face a similar chance of being blocked or challenged.

blocks.code:
# Synthetic login-challenge outcomes for GOOD users only, split by how they
# connect. A false positive here is a legitimate user who was blocked.
groups = {
    # group: (good users, good users blocked)
    "home broadband":          (50_000, 150),
    "mobile carrier (CGNAT)":  (30_000, 840),
    "shared library/campus":   (5_000, 260),
}
for g, (n, blocked) in groups.items():
    print(f"{g:24} false positive rate {blocked / n:.2%}")
# output:
# home broadband           false positive rate 0.30%
# mobile carrier (CGNAT)   false positive rate 2.80%
# shared library/campus    false positive rate 5.20%
blocks.caption: Synthetic false positive rates for honest users, by how they connect. Same model, very different burden.

blocks.title: Honest users blocked, by connection type (synthetic)

scenes.caption: One rule, three groups of honest users. Home broadband: 0.30% blocked.
Mobile users behind CGNAT: 2.80%, more than nine times higher, because the 'accounts per IP' signal counts their neighbours.
Shared campus or library connections: 5.20%. The overall rate (about 1.5%) hides that one group carries most of the friction.
An illustrative target after replacing raw IP counts with weighted links (lesson 10) and stepping up instead of blocking: 0.30%, 0.45% and 0.60%.

blocks.md:
**What to do:**

- **Measure by group**: false positive, challenge and appeal-overturn rates by country, language, device type, network type and, where lawful and available, by protected group.
- **Fix the signal, not only the threshold**: weight shared identifiers, and avoid features that encode where someone lives or what they can afford unless they truly predict fraud.
- **Prefer step-up to block** where groups are disproportionately hit, and make sure the step-up works for them (an SMS code is no help without a stable phone).
- **Document** each model's purpose, inputs, group metrics and review dates, so the next person can audit it.

Collect what measurably helps, keep it only as long as needed, and keep it out of other uses. Then measure who your false positives are: an acceptable average can hide an unacceptable burden on one group.

blocks.question: A rule's overall false positive rate is 1.5%. By group it is 0.3% for home broadband users and 5.2% for users on shared campus networks. What is the best next step?
options: Find which signal drives the gap (likely shared IP counts), weight or replace it, and consider step-up instead of block for that pattern
Raise the threshold for everyone until the average is below 1%
blocks.explain: The average hides a group burden. Fixing the proxy signal removes the cause; raising the threshold for everyone costs recall and may leave the gap in place; blocking networks makes it worse.

blocks.question: Your team proposes storing SHA-256 hashes of users' phone numbers 'so the data is anonymous'. Why is that not enough?
options: Phone numbers come from a small space, so anyone with the hashes can hash every possible number and match them
Hashes are larger than phone numbers
blocks.explain: Lesson 4's arithmetic applies: about 100 million candidates can be hashed quickly, reversing every hash. Hashed identifiers are pseudonymous personal data, not anonymous data.

lessons.title: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme

blocks.md:
Fraud is a game against people who watch your defences and change. The chip shift (lesson 13) moved fraud online; a per-IP limit moves attackers onto proxies; a 4-card rule teaches them to use 3. Every control has a half-life. Three habits keep a programme ahead.

**1. Ship rules carefully: shadow mode first.** A new rule runs in **shadow mode** (it evaluates and logs, but does not act) long enough to measure how often it would fire and how many of those were fraud, once labels mature. Then it goes live, often first on a small share of traffic. This avoids the classic outage of fraud teams: a rule that blocks 10% of good customers on a Friday night.

blocks.code:
# A new rule runs in shadow mode: it is evaluated and logged, never enforced.
def new_rule(e):
    return e["cards_per_device_1h"] >= 4 and e["amount"] < 5

events = [  # synthetic week; label arrives later (chargeback or not)
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 6, "amount": 1, "label": "fraud"},
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 5, "amount": 2, "label": "fraud"},
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 4, "amount": 3, "label": "good"},   # a family
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 1, "amount": 2, "label": "good"},
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 7, "amount": 40, "label": "fraud"},
    {"cards_per_device_1h": 1, "amount": 60, "label": "good"},
]
fired = [e for e in events if new_rule(e)]
tp = sum(e["label"] == "fraud" for e in fired)
total_fraud = sum(e["label"] == "fraud" for e in events)
print(f"would have fired {len(fired)} times, precision {tp}/{len(fired)},"
      f" recall {tp}/{total_fraud}")
# output:
# would have fired 3 times, precision 2/3, recall 2/3
blocks.caption: Shadow-mode evaluation of a new rule against later labels. It would have caught two of three frauds and hit one family sharing a tablet.

blocks.md:
**2. Watch for adaptation.** OWASP recommends that each defence produce volume metrics (detected and mitigated) so you can see failures and new attacks. Typical tells that attackers have adapted: a drop in a rule's hits without a drop in losses, losses moving to another product or payment method, attempts clustering just under a threshold, challenge solve rates rising suddenly. Some teams add **friction that does not reveal itself**: a delayed or randomised response, or a "pending review" status instead of an instant decline, so probing teaches less.

**3. Treat big attacks as incidents.** A credential stuffing wave, a card testing run or a promotion being farmed needs the same discipline as an intrusion: an owner, a channel, a timeline, containment, and a post-incident review.

blocks.title: An abuse incident: card testing on a Saturday (synthetic)

scenes.caption: Hour 0: a script starts testing cards on the 'save card' endpoint. Hour 1: the decline-rate alert (lesson 14) pages the on-call fraud engineer.
Hours 2 to 3: contain. Turn on a server-verified challenge for that endpoint and a per-IP limit on new customers. The attack falls away by hour 6.
Hours 6 to 24: recover. Refund the small payments that succeeded, stop retries on the fraudulent saved cards, tell the payment provider.
Hours 24 to 48: review. Why was that endpoint unprotected? Add it to the endpoint inventory, a test that fails if any card endpoint lacks a challenge, and a shadow rule for the pattern.

blocks.md:
**Running the programme.** A mature fraud and abuse function usually has:

- **An inventory of abusable flows** (signup, login, recovery, lookups, checkout, card setup, promotions, payouts, reviews, messaging), each with its owner, controls and metrics. Lesson 1's map is the start.
- **A signal platform**: velocity counters, device and network intelligence, the identity graph.
- **A decision layer**: model scores, rules with reason codes, shadow mode, per-flow thresholds set by expected cost.
- **Operations**: review queues, enforcement ladder, appeals, support playbooks.
- **Measurement**: matured loss, friction and group metrics, holdouts, overturn rates.
- **Partners**: payment providers, card networks, other platforms, law enforcement, and regulators when a data breach results.

**Practice, legally.** Use deliberately vulnerable applications and labs, never a real service's checkout, login or signup:

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security), free online labs; its business logic and authentication topics cover flawed limits, discounts, workflows and brute-force protection.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/), a deliberately insecure shop you run yourself; for its coupon, review and feedback challenges, write the server-side check and the detection signal that would have stopped each.
- Build the detectors in this course on your own synthetic logs: the success-rate and unknown-user monitor (lesson 3), bucketed velocity (lesson 7), union-find rings (lesson 10) and the cost-based thresholds (lessons 16 and 17).

For reading next: the [OWASP Automated Threats project](https://owasp.org/www-project-automated-threats-to-web-applications/) and Stripe's [card testing guide](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/card-testing).
Every control has a half-life. Launch in shadow mode, watch for adaptation through volume and loss metrics, run large attacks as incidents, and keep an inventory of every flow an attacker could farm.

blocks.question: A new rule looks great in a backtest. What is the safest way to launch it?
options: Turn it on for all traffic at once to stop fraud quickly
Run it in shadow mode to measure would-be hits against maturing labels, then enable it gradually
Announce the rule publicly as a deterrent
blocks.explain: Shadow mode measures false positives on live traffic without harming anyone; a gradual rollout limits damage if the backtest missed something.

blocks.question: A month after your 4-cards-per-device rule launched, its hits fell 90%, but fraud losses are unchanged and many devices now try exactly 3 cards. What does this indicate?
options: Attackers adapted to the threshold; losses, not rule hits, measure success
blocks.explain: Clustering just under a threshold with flat losses is classic adaptation. Combine the count with outcomes and amounts, avoid revealing exact thresholds, and track loss as the ground truth.
